title: Session catalog store port

intent.purpose: The store port of the session catalog: the TypeScript contract of the interface the catalog core (distributor) depends on, implemented by a PostgreSQL adapter and a SQLite adapter that must pass one shared conformance suite. It carries every write and read the approved Sessions API needs - sessions (create, lifecycle changes, rename, archive and unarchive, a run's outcome and spend, delete), asks (open, resolve, read one, list), and artifacts (seal, judge's verdict, attached links, list) - and nothing transport-shaped: no SQL, no HTTP, no driver types.
nonGoals: No SQL, no HTTP shapes, no node:sqlite or pg types: the adapters are the only code that knows the storage engine, and the HTTP adapter is the only code that knows the wire shapes (amountMicros as a decimal string, nextPageToken, problem documents).

Not a Lucene parser: the core parses q with a maintained parser and validates it against the collection's field set; this port carries the parsed, typed AST, and the adapters compile it to their own SQL.
Not the lifecycle channel: the channel that delivers a session's events is the core's business; this port is where the core writes them down.
Not the conformance suite itself: the suite's code is not exported here; the port's header states what the suite must prove.
Not process control or transcripts: no read starts a session's process, and the session's directory is the driver's, not the store's.
intent.audience: The distributor's catalog core, the PostgreSQL and SQLite adapter packages, and the shared conformance suite that must run both adapters.
consumers: The catalog core calls every method: it parses q into the AST, validates it against the field set, orders writes per session, caps pageSize, and maps each session's log events to these calls on rebuild.
The PostgreSQL adapter implements it over PostgreSQL (tsvector for full text; int8 or numeric for the micros).
The SQLite adapter implements it over SQLite (FTS5 for full text; INTEGER for the micros, read back as bigint).
The shared conformance suite drives both adapters on one shared corpus and asserts they agree.
guarantees: Idempotent replay: every write is guarded by a per-session watermark - the highest sequence applied - updated in the same transaction, and a write at or below it is a no-op that provably changes no row and no count.
Atomic lifecycle writes: a lifecycle write applies the row and its derived counts in one transaction, and a refused write changes nothing.
Integer money: micros are bigint from the core through the port; exact sums past 2^53 are preserved and asserted on both adapters by the conformance suite.
Stable pages: every list is a keyset with the list's key as the final tiebreak, and a cursor is bound to the (where, orderBy) that issued it.
Adapter parity: on the shared corpus both adapters agree on rows, order, and full-text matches.
Rebuild: deleting a session's rows and replaying its log through this port reproduces the live rows exactly.
Adapter-owned migrations: append-only, applied by migrate(), which the core calls at startup and memoizes once it succeeds.

choices.decision: The port is one interface of named methods grouped by the Sessions API's resources - sessions, asks, artifacts - each mirroring an HTTP verb (create, transition, rename, archive, run outcome, delete; open, resolve, read, list; seal, verdict, links, list), with no generic apply() and no per-key rev rules.

why.ref: Named methods per resource, or one apply(event) union?
why.text: Named methods; event writes take the event id
Named methods grouped by the same resources as the approved Sessions API, mirroring the HTTP verbs per resource, not RPC-style verbs or one generic apply().

choices.decision: Every write takes the reporting event's id and its position in the session's ordered write stream; the store holds a per-session watermark - the highest sequence applied - updated in the same transaction as the write, and a write at or below it is a no-op; delete and rebuild reset the watermark with the rows.

why.ref: How does the store decide a write is a replay, so it can no-op it?
why.text: You decide: use the suggested "Record applied event ids per session" and say in the why that the person delegated it
Idempotency: every write keyed by the reporting event's id; a replayed event is a no-op. Uniform idempotency, recorded by the store, never per-key rev rules.

choices.decision: A lifecycle write applies the row and its derived counts in one atomic transaction: recordRunOutcome cancels the session's pending asks, sums the run's spend and tokens, and sets lastActivity, lastRun and state together; a refused write changes nothing and no torn row is ever visible.

why.text: Transactions: a lifecycle change updates the row and its counts atomically.

why.ref: Does a run report its spend as a delta to sum, or the lifetime total to replace?
why.text: Per-run delta; the store sums it in

choices.decision: State writes split by provenance: transitionSession carries the channel's running|idle|stopped changes, archiveSession and unarchiveSession carry the person's archived|stopped writes, with the approved 409-while-running, 200-no-op and reactivation table; archived is left only by the transition to running.

why.text: Keep it RESTful: state moves as writes on the session resource, with the approved semantics.

PATCH: state accepts exactly archived (archive) and stopped (unarchive); 409 while running or waiting on a person; a write that changes nothing is a 200 no-op; invoking an archived session reactivates it (state -> running).
state is running, idle, stopped or archived; the lifecycle and the person's state writes are distinct channels of the same state.

choices.decision: Money is an ISO 4217 currency code with int64 micros carried as bigint in the port and the core; only the HTTP adapter encodes the approved wire shape (a decimal string), and the adapters convert at their edge.

why.ref: Money micros cross the port as what?
why.text: bigint

choices.decision: Spend and tokens are per-run deltas that the store sums, as integers, into the row's lifetime totals, so the row is a running sum and a replay is provably a no-op.

why.ref: Does a run report its spend as a delta to sum, or the lifetime total to replace?
why.text: Per-run delta; the store sums it in

why.ref: Money micros cross the port as what?
why.text: bigint

choices.decision: q is parsed in the core with a maintained Lucene parser - never hand-rolled, never in an adapter - into a typed AST with one value type per field (strings, enums, bigint micros, epoch-ms numbers, booleans); the adapters compile typed leaves to their own SQL, full text included, and fail loudly on a kind they do not know.

why.ref: Typed per-field values in the query AST, or parser-native strings?
why.text: Typed per field, one value type per collection
One list operation per collection takes a parsed query AST (Lucene grammar, parsed in the core, never in an adapter); adapters compile the AST to their own SQL.
q is a Lucene query parsed by a maintained Lucene parser - never hand-rolled; bare terms full-text search the list's documented fields; money compares in micros as an integer.
Discriminate unions with a kind, and say whether consumers must handle unknown members: an adapter meeting an unknown AST kind must fail loudly, since the core validated the query.

choices.decision: The three field sets are exactly the approved lists' q field sets, and the core validates a parsed query against them, so an unknown field is a 400 that never reaches a store.

why.text: Session list q field set: key, agent, title, state, createdAt, lastActivity, cost.currencyCode, cost.amountMicros, tokens.*, pendingAsks, oldestAskAt, lastRun.outcome; wildcards on key, agent, title and bare terms; bare terms full-text over title, key, last message.
Per-session ask list q field set: type, state, createdAt, resolvedAt, tool; bare terms full-text over the prompt question and the tool name.
Cross-session ask list q field set: session, type, state, createdAt, resolvedAt, tool.
Per-session artifact list q field set: kind, version, createdAt, verdict.passed; bare terms full-text over summary and outcome.
Cross-session artifact list q field set: session, kind, version, createdAt, verdict.passed.

choices.decision: There is one list operation per collection, taking the parsed AST, the list's allowed order, a page size and an opaque keyset cursor; the core composes the per-session views by folding the session term into where, since every row carries its session's key.

why.text: One list operation per collection taking a parsed query AST, an orderBy, a pageSize and a keyset cursor.
Every row carries its session's key, and session is a queryable field - so the per-session view is the one list operation with the session term folded in.

choices.decision: Each list has a small allowed set of orders with a fixed direction, the list's key is always the final tiebreak so pages are a stable keyset, and the order choice is part of what a cursor is bound to.

why.text: The session list accepts lastActivity (default, newest first), createdAt (newest first), oldestAskAt (oldest wait first); the ask lists createdAt (newest first per-session, oldest first cross-session); the artifact lists createdAt newest first. The list's key is always the final tiebreak, and the order choice is part of what a pageToken is bound to.

choices.decision: The cursor is opaque and bound to the (where, orderBy) pair that issued it, and an adapter must refuse a cursor it would not re-issue for that pair; presenting one under a changed query or order is the core's 400.

why.text: pageToken is an opaque keyset token bound to the (q, orderBy) pair that issued it; presenting it with a different query or order, or a token not issued by this deployment, is a 400.
Only a token this server would have issued: it must re-encode to itself - the self-verification an adapter must keep at the store port.

choices.decision: The adapters own the schema - append-only migrations, never edited once released - and the core calls migrate() at startup, memoizes success, and retries while the database is down, so the distributor can start before Postgres does.

why.text: Must decide and state: schema migration ownership.
Append-only: a released migration is never edited; the applied count lives in user_version - the adapter owns the schema.
The Postgres adapter takes pg_advisory_xact_lock(7461) around its migration - the adapter's own locking, invisible to the core.
Memoized once it succeeds, retried while the database is down, so the distributor can start before Postgres does.

choices.decision: Rebuild replays each session's log through the same port: deleteSession removes the session's rows and its watermark, and the core re-applies the session's recorded writes in order, mapping log events to these methods in the core, with the writer stopped first.

why.text: Must decide and state: rebuild - replay the log through the same port.
Replays every session log into the index; a log has one owner, so stop the distributor first.

choices.decision: One shared conformance suite proves, on one shared corpus: every write lands exactly its documented row, replays are no-ops with every row and count unchanged, the state machine applies, no-ops and refuses as documented, recordRunOutcome is one point of consistency, lists agree across every orderBy and a battery of ASTs covering every leaf kind and field, pages stay gap- and duplicate-free under interleaved writes, cursors are bound to (where, orderBy), FTS5 and tsvector agree on the documented text fields, integer sums stay exact past 2^53 micros, and rebuild reproduces the live rows exactly.

why.text: The two adapters must pass one shared conformance suite; decide and state what the suite must prove.

why.ref: Money micros cross the port as what?
why.text: bigint

why.ref: How does the store decide a write is a replay, so it can no-op it?
why.text: You decide: use the suggested "Record applied event ids per session" and say in the why that the person delegated it

choices.decision: Reads are pure: they read stored rows, create nothing, never start a session's process, and answer undefined for an absent row; a stopped session answers its stored rows instead of an empty list.

why.text: The port carries everything the REST surface needs; every read in that surface comes from the catalog and no read starts a session's process.
Every read in this API is served from the session catalog; no read scans session directories or starts a process.

choices.decision: Dates are epoch ms in the port and the core; the HTTP adapter converts to the wire's RFC 3339.

why.text: Facts keep epoch ms and the wire speaks RFC 3339 - the same split: the port and the core keep epoch ms, the HTTP adapter converts.

choices.decision: resolution.by is the server-set actor - a person (id present) or the tailnet (no id) - filled by the core from the request's credential, never from a body, and never invented by the store.

why.text: The server sets the ask's state to resolved, stamps resolvedAt, and fills resolution.by from the request's credential - the body never carries an identity.
A person the reverse proxy authenticated (the username its identity header carries) or the tailnet itself (no header): { kind: person|tailnet, id } with id present only for a person.

choices.decision: The judge's verdict and attached links arrive after the seal, through their own writes - updateArtifactVerdict and addArtifactLink - because the REST surface serves and filters on verdict.passed and extensions attach links after the fact.

why.text: The judge attaches its verdict to a sealed version after the seal (attachVerdict).
An extension attaches a link to a sealed version after the fact (attachLink).
The REST surface serves links on the row and filters on verdict.passed - so both must be writable through the port.

choices.decision: Open fields that carry arbitrary JSON - a resolved approval's tool arguments, kept as the audit trail - use a named recursive Json, keeping the port free of any.

why.text: Resolved asks keep their tool arguments: the record of what was approved is the audit trail.
Name types and export only the ones that live in a public signature: the recursive Json value is named and exported because it appears in AskRow and openAsk.
